title: How School Districts Can Prepare for Midyear Staffing Gaps
summary: Learn how school districts can prepare for midyear staffing gaps, manage substitute coverage, and maintain student services with practical staffing strategies.
body_markdown:
Even with careful planning at the start of the school year, staffing needs can change quickly. Unexpected leaves, teacher absences, rising special education caseloads, and unfilled positions can leave school districts scrambling to maintain classroom coverage and student services.


These challenges often become more noticeable after holiday breaks, during cold and flu season, and as districts approach spring evaluations and end-of-year deadlines.


While some vacancies are unavoidable, there are steps school leaders can take to anticipate staffing needs, respond more quickly, and minimize disruptions to students and staff.


Drawing on our experience supporting school districts, the RCM team shares practical ways to prepare for midyear staffing challenges.


## Recognize the Early Signs of Staffing Gaps


Staffing needs can shift throughout the school year, and early signs of coverage challenges may emerge before a vacancy becomes more difficult to fill. Recognizing these changes can help districts plan ahead and respond more effectively.


**Our education staffing team recommends watching for several common indicators:**


- Increasing staff absences: More frequent callouts or anticipated extended leaves can put pressure on existing coverage plans.
- Difficulty filling substitute requests: Unfilled same-day requests may indicate that the available substitute pool is no longer meeting demand.
- Greater reliance on internal staff: Teachers, support staff, or administrators repeatedly stepping in to cover vacancies can signal a growing staffing concern.
- Rising student service needs: Increased referrals, evaluations, or students qualifying for specialized services can create additional demand for special education teachers and related service providers.


Reviewing these patterns regularly can help districts identify where[additional staffing support](https://www.rcmt.com/resources/blogs/how-to-choose-school-based-staffing-partner/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) may be needed.


## Plan Ahead for Known and Seasonal Staffing Needs


Some staffing needs can be anticipated well before a position becomes vacant. Reviewing historical absence patterns, upcoming leaves, professional development calendars, and current caseloads can help districts prepare for periods of higher demand.


For example, schools may experience increased substitute needs following winter break or during seasonal illness. Special education teams may also face greater pressure in the spring as they work to complete evaluations and meet service requirements before the end of the academic year.


The RCM Education Staffing team encourages districts to maintain regular communication with their staffing partners throughout the year, even when positions are currently filled. Sharing anticipated vacancies, expected caseload changes, and upcoming coverage needs gives recruiters more time to identify qualified professionals.


For specialized positions that are consistently difficult to fill, planning should begin in the spring or early summer for the following school year. Maintaining an active substitute pool and reviewing staffing needs regularly can also help districts respond more effectively when unexpected absences occur.


## Respond Quickly When a Staffing Gap Occurs


When an unexpected vacancy arises, timely communication can make a meaningful difference in how quickly a district can secure coverage.


One of the most common challenges our team encounters is receiving staffing requests without complete assignment details or after internal coverage options have already been exhausted.


Having the right information available from the beginning allows a staffing partner to focus recruiting efforts on professionals who meet the district’s needs.


### What to Have Ready When Requesting Staffing Support


**Before reaching out, districts should be prepared to share:**


- Position responsibilities and required qualifications or licensure
- School location, schedule, working hours, and anticipated assignment length
- Student population, caseload size, and service requirements, when applicable
- Whether the need is immediate, temporary, or expected to become long term
- Any district-specific clearance, onboarding, or background check requirements


Clear expectations also help prevent delays caused by changes to schedules, responsibilities, or qualifications after recruiting has begun.


For special education and related services positions, districts should prioritize maintaining required services under students’ Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) while arranging appropriate coverage.


## Consider Flexible Staffing Options


A traditional full-time placement may be the right solution for some vacancies, but districts can also benefit from having additional coverage options available.


Depending on the role and the needs of the school, several approaches may help maintain services and classroom support.


### Daily and Long-Term Substitute Teachers


An established substitute pool helps districts respond to unexpected absences and planned leaves. For longer-term vacancies, securing a consistent educator can also help maintain classroom routines and instructional continuity.


### Dedicated Floaters and Roving Substitutes


Schools experiencing frequent daily absences may benefit from dedicated floaters who report regularly and provide coverage wherever it is needed.


Our team has also seen how these professionals can support testing, school events, administrative needs, and before- or after-school programs when classroom coverage is not required.


### Temporary, Part-Time, and Virtual Services


For hard-to-fill specialties, temporary or part-time providers may help districts address service needs while continuing to recruit for longer-term positions.


Virtual services may also be an option for certain specialties, such as speech-language therapy, particularly in areas where access to qualified providers is limited. Districts should evaluate whether virtual delivery is appropriate for the students and services involved.


## Keep Student Services and Continuity in Focus


Staffing gaps affect more than daily schedules. Prolonged vacancies can disrupt classroom routines, increase demands on existing staff, and make it more difficult for students to receive consistent instruction and support.


These challenges can be especially significant in special education, where staffing shortages may affect the delivery of IEP-required services.


Our education staffing team frequently sees demand for special education teachers, paraprofessionals, Board Certified Behavior Analysts (BCBAs), speech-language pathologists, occupational therapists, and other specialized providers.


One-to-one paraprofessional and nursing vacancies can be particularly urgent when students depend on that support to attend school and participate safely in their educational programs.


When districts anticipate these needs and communicate them early, they give themselves more time to find qualified professionals and maintain consistent services.
